title: Bun Rewrites 535K Lines of Zig into Rust in Four Months, Eliminates Numerous Memory Leaks
gist: Bun creator Jarred Sumner used a pre-release version of Claude Fable 5, orchestrated across roughly 50 workflows and 64 parallel instances, to port 535,496 lines of Zig to Rust in four months for about $165,000 in API tokens, shipping v1.4.0 with 128 longstanding bugs fixed and memory use plateauing at 609 MB instead of climbing past 6.7 GB. Zig creator Andrew Kelley publicly attacked the result as a million lines of unreviewed slop.

insights.claim: A 535,496-line Zig codebase was ported to Rust in four months against an original estimate of a full year, inverting the conventional wisdom that large rewrites are a terrible idea because they freeze bugfixes, security fixes and feature development.
insights.speaker: Bruno Couriol
insights.so_what: If rewrite duration collapses from years to months, the calculus on legacy language migration and technical debt changes across the industry.
insights.quote: Historically, rewrites are a terrible idea. […] Bun is 535,496 lines of Zig. A rewrite in another language would take a small team of engineers a full year.

insights.claim: Reaching a fully passing test suite consumed 5.9 billion uncached input tokens, 690 million output tokens and 72 billion cached input token reads, costing roughly $165,000 at API pricing, against an estimate of three engineers with full codebase context working for about a year.
insights.speaker: Bruno Couriol
insights.so_what: The clearest published substitution ratio yet between token spend and senior engineering headcount - roughly $165k against several million dollars of labour.
insights.quote: around $165,000 at API pricing. By hand, I think this would’ve taken 3 engineers with full context on the codebase about a year.
insights.locator: Getting to the full test suite passing

insights.claim: At peak the system generated roughly 1,300 lines of code per minute and logged up to 695 commits an hour, distributed across four workspace shards running 16 agents each for 64 Claude instances in parallel.
insights.speaker: Bruno Couriol
insights.so_what: Concrete throughput ceiling for parallel agentic engineering, and a demand signal for inference capacity sold to coding workloads.
insights.locator: The effort was ultimately distributed across four workspace shards

insights.claim: Massive parallelisation of implementation tasks forces two infrastructure problems that gate throughput: concurrent updates to a shared codebase and starvation of limited computing resources.
insights.speaker: Bruno Couriol
insights.so_what: The bottleneck for agent swarms is coordination and capacity, not model intelligence - where tooling value will accrue.
insights.locator: The implementation process efficiency massively leverages the parallelization

insights.claim: Bun was acquired by Anthropic in December 2025, making this rewrite simultaneously a product migration and a flagship demonstration of the acquirer's pre-release model.
insights.speaker: Bruno Couriol
insights.so_what: Read the published metrics as both engineering evidence and marketing for the model vendor that owns the project.
insights.locator: Bun was acquired by Anthropic in December 2025.

themes.theme: The harness, not the model, did the work

insights.claim: The enabling precondition for the port was that Bun's test suite is written in TypeScript and therefore does not depend on the runtime's implementation language, giving more than one million assertions that could validate a translation into any target language.
insights.speaker: Bruno Couriol
insights.so_what: Verification assets, not model capability, decide which codebases are portable by AI - a screening criterion for where this playbook can be repeated.
insights.quote: Bun’s own test suite is written in TypeScript which means it doesn’t depend on the runtime’s programming language.

insights.claim: Two written artefacts were identified as key success factors: PORTING.md describing the mapping from Zig patterns and types to Rust ones, and LIFETIMES.tsv describing the lifetimes of every struct field in the codebase.
insights.speaker: Bruno Couriol
insights.so_what: Upfront machine-readable domain mapping is the reproducible part of the playbook, and the part that cannot be bought from a model vendor.
insights.locator: PORTING.md (describing the mapping from Zig to Rust)

insights.claim: Roles were strictly separated: an implementer agent translated files while two adversarial reviewer agents ran in isolated context windows with access only to file diffs and the sole task of finding bugs and behavioural divergences, with a separate fixer agent applying remedies.
insights.speaker: Bruno Couriol
insights.so_what: Isolated adversarial review is the emerging quality-control pattern for agentic engineering, and a template for evaluating agent platforms.
insights.quote: The implementer doesn’t review. The reviewer doesn’t implement.
insights.locator: An implementer would then use those files

insights.claim: After each error the team improved the implementation process rather than manually fixing the produced code, treating the generation loop rather than the artefact as the unit of maintenance.
insights.speaker: Bruno Couriol
insights.so_what: Process-level rather than artefact-level debugging is what makes agent output scale - a signature of teams doing this well.
insights.locator: The implementation loop would be improved after each error

insights.claim: The planning phase was described as critical to success and had to result in key challenges being anticipated and mitigated before implementation began.
insights.speaker: Bruno Couriol
insights.so_what: Front-loaded planning is the cheap input that determines whether large agentic projects converge at all.
insights.locator: The constant process improvement revealed useful patterns

insights.claim: The stated motivation for choosing Rust was that use-after-free, double-free and forgotten frees in error paths become compiler errors with automatic cleanup through Drop, converting a documentation problem into a build-time one.
insights.speaker: Bruno Couriol
insights.so_what: Language-level enforcement over process discipline is the argument driving continued Rust adoption in systems software.
insights.quote: Compiler errors are a better feedback loop than a style guide.

insights.claim: The Rust implementation shipped in Bun v1.4.0 in August 2026 resolved 128 longstanding bugs that were present in v1.3.14.
insights.speaker: Bruno Couriol
insights.so_what: A quantified defect reduction is the strongest available evidence that mass AI translation can improve rather than degrade quality.
insights.locator: According to the Bun team, the resulting Rust implementation

insights.claim: In-process bundling tests running 2,000 consecutive Bun.build() operations plateaued stably at 609 MB under Rust rather than climbing past 6.7 GB, while HTTP throughput increased only 2% to 5%.
insights.speaker: Bruno Couriol
insights.so_what: The payoff was memory safety and stability, not speed - the right expectation to set for comparable Rust migrations.

insights.claim: The mechanical nature of the port introduced 19 subtle semantic regressions rooted in syntactic similarities between Zig and Rust, requiring 11 rounds of security review from Claude Code Security plus 24/7 coverage-guided fuzzing of every parser that produced 15 further pull requests.
insights.speaker: Bruno Couriol
insights.so_what: Syntactic look-alikes are where machine translation silently fails, so the safety net costs real money and must be budgeted alongside the port itself.
insights.locator: The mechanical nature of the port introduced 19 subtle semantic regressions

insights.claim: Zig creator Andrew Kelley argues the framing presents a false dichotomy between a style guide and a language feature, misdirecting readers from the main way bugs are actually eliminated, which is dedicating engineering resources to the problem.
insights.speaker: Bruno Couriol
insights.so_what: The strongest counter-argument to the memory-safety migration narrative: the gains may be attention, not language.
insights.quote: The sleight of hand misdirects the reader away from the main way bugs are eliminated: by dedicating engineering resources to it.
insights.locator: Zig creator Andrew Kelley published a sharply critical reaction

insights.claim: Kelley identifies an internal contradiction in the justification: the test suite is claimed insufficient to catch bugs in the original Zig code yet sufficient to validate a million lines of unreviewed machine-generated Rust.
insights.speaker: Bruno Couriol
insights.so_what: Test-suite sufficiency is the load-bearing assumption of every AI mass-migration pitch, and it is contestable.
insights.quote: It’s not sufficient to catch bugs in Zig code but it is sufficient to catch bugs in 1 million lines of unreviewed slop?
insights.locator: Zig creator Andrew Kelley published a sharply critical reaction

insights.claim: Merging over one million lines of machine-transpiled code makes Bun an industry canary for whether massive LLM-generated codebases can remain maintainable across the software engineering lifecycle.
insights.speaker: Bruno Couriol
insights.so_what: A specific, dated experiment to track: Bun's maintenance burden over the next few releases is evidence for or against mass AI code generation.
